title: An Invitation to Grow
author: Steve Karandy
summary: Steve Karandy previews the first chapter of his new book, Brewing Innovation, by telling how wrestling coach Joe Bena invited him into a sport he knew nothing about with the promise that the coaches would teach him everything he needed to know. He draws a leadership lesson for school leaders bringing AI into their buildings: asking people to try something unfamiliar takes more than demonstrating a tool, because leaders must pay attention to the person taking that step. He argues that innovation is a mindset and a culture, not a set of apps, and that leaders must follow through after the announcement by building skills. The post closes with a practical step for the week, inviting a colleague to work through a small task together, and with reflection questions about who once gave the reader that kind of invitation. Part of the post is a book promotion, but the leadership argument stands on its own.
points: Asking people to try something unfamiliar requires attending to the person, not just showing what the tool can do.
Leaders should make room for the person who says they know nothing, since that admission gives a place to start.
Innovation is a mindset and culture, so leaders must follow through after the initial announcement by building skills and knowledge.
The practical step is to invite one colleague to a small task, ask what help they want, and try an approved tool together honestly.
Grit and a leader's belief in someone taking a first step matter more than prior experience.
quotes: Asking someone to try something unfamiliar takes more than showing them what a tool can do. We have to pay attention to the person being asked to take that step.
As we bring AI into our schools, I think we need to make room for the person who says, “I don’t know anything about this.” That admission gives us a place to start.
We have to remember that innovation is a mindset and building a culture around that is more than just tools and apps.

As leaders we need to think about the work, not just the initial initiative announcement. We see it too often when something is introduced and there is no follow through, we need to help build their skills and knowledge to apply it to their practice.
Choose an approved tool, make time to try it together, and talk honestly about what worked and what did not.
While technology advances and improves, we must remember that it is humanity that remains at the center of leadership.
